questions.question: What do semantic layout elements give you that div does not?
questions.answer: Meaning and landmarks. header, nav, main, aside, and footer expose roles that screen readers can jump between, and they help SEO and code readability. div carries no semantics.

questions.question: How many main elements should a page have, and where can main not be nested?
questions.answer: Exactly one visible main per page. It should not be inside header, nav, aside, or footer, because main represents the unique content of the document.

questions.question: Explain section versus article with a test.
questions.answer: An article is self-contained and could be syndicated on its own, like a post or comment. A section is a thematic part of the page and usually has a heading. If it would make sense in an RSS feed alone, it is an article.

questions.question: Which elements create which landmarks?
questions.answer: header → banner, nav → navigation, main → main, aside → complementary, footer → contentinfo, search → search. A section becomes a region only when it has an accessible name.

questions.question: Why is a section without a heading usually the wrong choice?
questions.answer: An unnamed section is not exposed as a region landmark, so it adds no navigation value. Without a heading it is just a generic box — use a div unless the group has a real theme and name.

questions.question: Does using header and footer automatically style them?
questions.answer: No. Semantic elements have only default browser styles; you must style them with CSS. Semantics describe meaning, not appearance.
